title: 128k Long-Context Performance Deep Dive - Hermes Corp
summary: Redwood SEs walked Hermes through runtime design and optimizations for 128k+ token workloads. Discussion covered chunking / retrieval strategies to avoid quadratic attention costs, KV cache segmentation and disk-backed fallback, batching shapes and latency/throughput tradeoffs, quantization approaches (GPTQ/4-bit) and quality tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem networking and storage considerations. Agreed next steps: run Hermes sample benchmark, share quantization guide and kernel perf slides, and schedule an on-prem pilot kickoff.
next_steps: Redwood to run 3 staged benchmarks on Hermes sample corpus (latency + throughput + regression) and share results
Send quantization / GPTQ profile recommendations and kernel compatibility notes
Share security/compliance pack (SOC2 artifacts, KMS integration notes) with Marta
Schedule on-prem kickoff with infra team (Ming, Rajiv) - target week of 2026-05-04
action_items: Diego Ramos: prepare benchmark harness and initial perf dashboard by 2026-04-27
Asha Patel: send pricing/committed capacity options and pilot contract template by 2026-04-24
Ming Zhao: draft VPC/network architecture notes for Hermes on-prem by 2026-05-01
Tom Nguyen: provide sample corpus + expected query distribution by 2026-04-23
transcript: [00:00] Asha (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll kick off, quick intros - I'm Asha from Redwood, Diego and Ming are our infra folks, and from Hermes could you do quick intros?
[00:18] Lena (Hermes): Sure, I'm Lena, I own the ML platform. Rajiv's our SRE and Marta handles security. Tom's the NLP lead on the project.

[00:30] Diego (SE): Quick agenda: go over long-context runtime strategy for 128k, chunking options, kv cache behavior, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and then VPC/on-prem nuances. We'll keep it technical and save procurement stuff for after.

[01:05] Tom (Hermes): Great. Our main ask: we need to support ingesting entire doc stores up to 100k-200k tokens for context windows for summarization and Q&A. Latency target is interactive-ish: 1.5-3s for short answers, but we can tolerate longer for heavy summarization. Throughput is also important because we run batch jobs overnight.

[01:40] Diego: So first principle — attention is quadratic in sequence length. For 128k contexts you can't naively run full attention end-to-end. We typically combine strategies: chunking with retrieval, hierarchical attentions, and KV cache segmentation to avoid reprocessing prefixes.
[02:10] Rajiv: When you say KV cache segmentation, do you mean sharding cache across GPUs, or spilling to disk? Concerned about memory footprint and cross-node traffic.

[02:25] Ming: Both. For very long contexts we recommend a hybrid: keep a hot KV cache for most-recent active segments in GPU RAM, and have a compressed disk-backed cold cache that can be streamed in parallel. We use a small async prefetcher to hide I/O latency. Disk-backed KV can be compressed with quantized keys and chunk-level embeddings to reduce bytes moved.
[03:00] Tom: Any specifics on chunk size? We've tried 4k and 8k chunks previously but haven't scaled to 128k.

[03:15] Diego: Chunk size is workload dependent. For retrieval-heavy tasks, smaller chunks (1k-4k tokens) give better granularity for hits but increase meta overhead. For summarization where you need wide context, larger chunks (8k-16k) reduce edges. Also consider overlapping sliding windows (e.g., 25% overlap) to handle cross-boundary attention — that reduces missing context at boundaries at cost of duplicate compute.
[04:05] Lena: Sliding windows sound expensive. How do you mitigate double computation?

[04:15] Diego: We use prefix caching and reuse KV states. For overlapping windows we only recompute the overlap region's attention once by aligning cache indices. Also, when possible, apply selective attention (sparse attention) to reduce complexity — e.g., local attention + global tokens or a routed global attention matrix. There's also memory-compressed attention variants (we mentioned FLASH-attn, flashAttn, call it a lot of names in perf notes) that are much faster on A100/Green cards.
[05:00] Marta (Hermes): From the security side, if we spill KV to disk on-prem, how is that encrypted and audited? We need KMS integration and SOC2 artifacts.

[05:15] Ming: For private deployments we support KMS/HSM integration. Disk-backed caches can be encrypted at rest with customer keys and we surface audit logs for cache access. We'll include the compliance pack in the follow-up. For hosted, we keep caches in encrypted managed volumes and rotate keys.
[05:50] Tom: Does the runtime support attention optimizations like FlashAttention and rotary/ALiBi? Any gotchas with model variants?

[06:05] Diego: Yes, runtime supports FlashAttention, FlashAttn2, multiple rotary implementations and ALiBi for positional handling. The main gotcha is kernel compatibility: some quantized kernels or certain custom ops need model conversion or a small kernel fallback. We'll include a kernel compatibility matrix in the docs. Also note that very long sequences sometimes require switching to recompute-mode or rotary with larger base to maintain numerical stability.
[07:00] Rajiv: On batching — what's the tradeoff between large batch sizes for throughput vs. tail latency for interactive queries?

[07:12] Diego: We recommend hybrid batching: keep a low-latency lane for single-shot interactive requests (small batch / immediate scheduling) and a throughput lane batcher for bulk jobs. For long-context, batching increases memory pressure due to KV duplication. We do dynamic batching that coalesces compatible sequence shapes and reuses KV pointers rather than duplicating caches where possible.
[08:00] Tom: How do you estimate per-token latency for a 128k window? Have you run benchmarks?

[08:12] Diego: We've run internal benchmarks — end-to-end depends on chunking pattern. For example: with 16k chunks + efficient prefetching and FlashAttention, token generation latency for causal decoding is within 30-60ms per token on high-end GPUs in dedicated setups. But full-document summarization that needs to scan 128k will incur a multi-second upfront cost for encoding and retrieval. We'll share our benchmark slides; the spreadsheet link has permutations we run.
[08:55] Lena: Can Redwood do an initial pilot with our sample corpus? We'd like to see the latency numbers specifically for our docs, and also regression tests on quality after quantization.
[09:10] Asha: Yes, Diego will run the harness. We'll need sample docs and expected Q/A sets. Tom, you mentioned you'll provide the corpus — thanks.
[09:25] Tom: I'll upload ~10k docs and a representative query distribution to the sheet after the call.

[09:40] Diego: On quantization: GPTQ-style 4-bit is what we often recommend for production cost reduction. It's great for throughput but you must validate for generation/regression. Some models degrade on instruction-following after extreme quant — per-layer mixed precision helps: keep first and last layers in 8-bit or FP16 and quantize the middle layers to 4-bit.
[10:20] Tom: Do you provide automated quantization pipelines or do we need to run GPTQ offline?

[10:30] Ming: We offer tooling and recommended configs plus a managed quantization pipeline for private deployments. For hosted, we test quantized variants and publish Redwood-verified profiles. For on-prem we can assist with an offline GPTQ run and validate outputs against your eval sets.
[11:00] Rajiv: Network: if we run on-prem in our VPC, what NICs and interconnects are recommended? We worry about cross-node KV traffic and RDMA.

[11:12] Ming: For low-latency KV sharding you want 100GbE with RoCE or NVLink for multi-GPU boxes. RDMA helps reduce CPU overhead for KV fetches. If you can't do RDMA, ensure your NICs and kernel stacks are tuned and use our async prefetchers to batch disk and network I/O. We'll provide an ops checklist for the NIC/driver/kernel settings.
[12:00] Marta: For compliance, we need audit trails when requests access user data slices. Can Redwood surface per-request cache access logs?

[12:12] Diego: Yes — we have per-request tracing which includes which cache shards were hit, token ranges accessed, and decision logs for routing. Those traces can be exported to your SIEM and stored per your retention policy.
[12:45] Lena: In terms of rollouts, what does canary look like for a big kernel change (e.g., enabling flashAttn2)?

[12:55] Diego: Canary is multi-step: internal A/B on a small percentage of traffic, run regression sets (both perf and quality), escalate if tail-latency is acceptable. We also provide automatic fallback to compatible non-optimized kernel if perf regressions are detected.
[13:30] Tom: We have a use-case that uses structured tool calling while keeping 80k tokens in context. Any special considerations?

[13:42] Diego: Tool-calling leads to structured outputs and often short responses; you can route those to the low-latency lane. For long context follow-ups, we preserve KV across calls. Be mindful of KV cache growth: implement TTL or LRU eviction policies to bound memory.
[14:20] Rajiv: For batch overnight summarization — does Redwood recommend horizontally scaling or using bigger GPUs per node?

[14:30] Ming: Both can work. Horizontal scaling helps with parallelism and throughput but increases cross-node KV complexity. Using bigger GPUs (more memory per device) reduces cross-node traffic and simplifies KV locality. If you have a large dataset and tight windowing, we recommend GPUs with >80GB or orchestrated model parallelism with local KV affinity.
[15:05] Tom: Any notes on embeddings + retrieval hybrid vs full attention? We considered retrieving top-k passages and concatenating vs letting the model attend globally.

[15:18] Diego: Retrieval + concatenation is often the most cost-effective: run a dense retriever to pull top-k passages (with overlapping context) and feed those in prioritized order. For truly global tasks (e.g., cross-document synthesis) you still need hierarchical summarization: first summarize chunks, then summarize summaries, so the model doesn't process all raw tokens at once.
[16:00] Marta: What about consistency and determinism when using quantized models and caching? We need reproducible outputs for audits.

[16:10] Ming: Determinism can be affected by mixed-precision, parallel scheduling and randomized kernels. For audit-critical paths we run a deterministic mode (single-threaded kernels / fixed seeds) and record seed and kernel versions in logs. That comes with perf cost but gives reproducibility.
[17:00] Asha: Quick pause — any other infra-level questions?
[17:08] Rajiv: How do you measure and surface tail-latency per-request for long-context flows?

[17:20] Diego: We use per-token and per-request histograms, and break down time by stages: retrieval, encode, attention compute, decode. Dashboards show p50/p90/p99 and we correlate with batch shapes and cache hit rates.
[18:00] Tom: Are there known model architecture gotchas for 128k context? Like attention memory blowups with some decoder-only vs encoder-decoder models?

[18:12] Diego: Decoder-only models with causal masks often have simpler KV caching semantics, but cross-attention in encoder-decoder can be used when you want separate encoder pass for the whole doc. For extremely long context we sometimes run a compression encoder pass (e.g., pooling/summary tokens) and then a decoder pass — that gives lower compute at cost of possibly losing fine-grained interactions.
[19:00] Lena: License/ops: For on-prem, do we get the same performance features as hosted? Any features gated to Redwood cloud?

[19:10] Asha: Core runtime features are available for Private/on-prem with enterprise licensing. Some managed observability and automatic upgrades remain controlled by Redwood control plane in the managed private mode; fully air-gapped installs are possible but require ops support contract.
[19:45] Tom: For quantized kernels, do you expose kernel-level metrics? We want to correlate per-layer perf with quality drop.
[19:55] Diego: Yes — we instrument per-layer timings and memory. The perf dashboard can show which layers dominate walltime under the quantized kernel.
[20:20] Marta: Anything special about multi-tenant hosts and data leakage? If we use dedicated capacity, how do you isolate caches and memory?

[20:32] Ming: Dedicated pools are single-tenant; caches are per-tenant; we also provide hardware isolation options. For host-level multitenancy we do strong RBAC and memory zeroization on evict. We'll provide details in the security pack.

[21:00] Diego: Now, concrete perf knobs you can tune: chunk size, overlap percentage, batch shape caps, KV TTL, quantization profile (4-bit mixed), attention kernel selection, and prefetch window size. We recommend running the grid in the spreadsheet to find Pareto points.
[21:40] Tom: On the spreadsheet, can you add a column for expected token-distribution (doc-heavy vs query-heavy)?
[21:52] Diego: Yes — add that and we'll run targeted benchmarks. Also include a small eval set for quality checks post-quant.
[22:20] Lena: Timelines — if we start pilot this month, how long before we see results?

[22:30] Asha: Typical pilot runs: 1 week for setup + sample ingestion, 1 week for basic perf runs, 1 week for quant/quality validation. So 3 weeks to initial results if Hermes can provide the corpus promptly.
[23:00] Tom: One final question — for really huge contexts (200k) do you recommend a different model family or is the runtime the limiting factor?

[23:12] Diego: Both model choice and runtime matter. Some models are architected with chunking-friendly attention or have longer context variants; others will need more aggressive chunking. Runtime can only mitigate so much — horizontally distributing the context encoding and then merging summaries is often the practical path.
[24:00] Lena: OK, let's recap next steps quickly

[24:06] Asha: Recap: Hermes to upload corpus and expected query distribution; Diego to run benchmark harness and return perf dashboard; Ming to share VPC/on-prem ops checklist; Asha to send commercial/pilot docs and security pack to Marta. We'll target Kirk-week May 4th for an on-prem kickoff. Any objections?
[24:40] Marta: No objections, thanks all. Appreciate the detail.
[24:50] Asha: Great — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the spreadsheet link. Thanks everyone — we'll close out here.
[25:00] (call ends)
